articles.headline: Billings County Convention.
articles.text:
Notice is hereby given that on the 25th day of October, at two p. m., a convention will be held in the Town hall for the purpose of placing in nomination a full county ticket for the coming election. A full turn-out is desired.

MANY VOTERS.
articles.summary: Notice of a Billings County convention in the Town hall on October 25 to nominate a full county ticket.

articles.text: Theodore Roosevelt was recently nominated by the Republicans of New York city as their candidate for mayor and has accepted the nomination. New York is and has been strongly democratic, but the County and Tammany Democrats are at swords' points and there are already five or six candidates for the office. The Republicans are heartily united on Roosevelt and it would not be strange if business as New York's mayor would prevent him from being present at our spring round-up. If the Bad Lands "cow punchers" could help him out with their votes, he would go in with a rush.
articles.summary: Theodore Roosevelt has been nominated by New York City Republicans for mayor; the paper jokes Bad Lands cowpunchers' votes would put him in with a rush.

articles.text: The candidacy of Supt. Green on the democratic ticket for the legislature is a conundrum to every paper in the district. When a rail-road man is running for office, the cry is always raised that the rail-road has a job it wants to push through. In this case, however, it would have been far easier for the rail-road to have nominated an outside man on the Republican ticket and no cry of jobbery would have been raised. Mr. Green is an ardent Democrat and it looks as though he has consented to be sacrificed for pure love of party. The break in the Republican ranks, owing to the enmity caused by the Bismarck convention, may make some difference on the vote, but we do not think that even Mr. Green thinks he stands any chance of election. He would make an able representative, but if elected, his railroad position would badly handicap him in any legislation he desired.
articles.summary: Comment on railroad Supt. Green's Democratic candidacy for the legislature.

articles.text: There is much uncertainty as to the precinct boundaries and probably will be until the lines are better known. The county has been divided by the commissioners into three voting precincts, by east and west lines. The northern precinct is No. 1, and at the coming election elects a commissioner for one year. It begins on a line running east and west near the Co.'s horse corrall below Lamb's ranch and extends to the northern boundary of the county. All voters within these limits will vote at Tompkins' ranch. Precinct No. 2 is the Medora district and extends from the south line of precinct No. 1, to a line running east and west through a point about a quarter of a mile north of the Logging Camp. It elects a commissioner for two years. All voters in this precinct will vote at the Court House in Medora. Precinct No. 3 elects a commissioner for three years and includes all the county south of precinct No. 2. The polling-place is the home ranch of the Little Missouri Horse Co. In the above, concerning the election of commissioners for different terms in the different precints, it should not be constrned that each precinct nominates and elects its own commissioner. All candidates are nominated and elected by the county at large, but a commissioner must be chosen from each precinct. The terms of office were decided by lot.
articles.summary: Description of the three Billings County voting precincts, their polling places and commissioner terms.

articles.text: The Bismarck convention for the nomination of candidates for the legislature, was an eye-opener to those not acquainted with the arts of the wily politician. The west-Missouri country has been allotted a member of the lower house heretofore, a representation that our population demands. It was thought then, that the only contest would be as to the candidate nominated by the west-Missouri country. This was decided at Mandan by the nomination of Maj. T. J. Mitchell, who, although not Billings county's first choice, would probably have made a good representative. At the legislative convention held at Bismarck last Saturday, the claims of the west-Missouri country were entirely ignored and Alexander Hughes of Burleigh was nominated for the council and E. A. Williams of Burleigh and W. F. Steele, were nominated for the house. The manner of bringing these nominations about displayed the finest piece of political wire-pulling that Dakota has ever seen. There were thirty-five delegates to the convention and although Burleigh county voted for Mitchell, he was defeated by a vote of eighteen to seventeen. The Morton delegates objected strongly to this vote and openly charged Burleigh with treachery. On the face of things, Burleigh had acted in a perfectly honorable manner and her delegates pointed to their vote to prove it. But he who judges politics and especially Dakota politics, by outward signs, shows himself the rankest kind of a political tyro. It is well known that Bismarck is by no means secure in her possession of the capital and that a determined effort will be made this winter to remove it to some point in central or southern Dakota. To oppose such a measure, Bismarck wants to be represented by her ablest workers and the three chosen are absolutely the three best men in the district to work for Bismarck's interests. These are the actual facts in the case and one is not long in seeing the fine Italian hand of the Burleigh county ring which used the outside counties as a cat's paw with which to draw its chestnuts out of the fire. The matter does not affect Billings county particularly, except that it practically disfranchises the whole west-Missouri country, leaving us without a representation which rightfully belongs to us. The scheme was a good one, but Burleigh county will some day be sat on hard by Morton county, whether she is guilty of treachery or not.
articles.summary: Editorial on the Bismarck legislative convention, where Burleigh County men were nominated and the west-Missouri country's candidate Maj. T. J. Mitchell lost 18 to 17.

articles.text: The name of Howard Eaton has been prominently mentioned as a candidate for commissioner from precinct No. 1. He absolutely declines however, and favors D. C. Rowe strongly for the position. The Beaver creek country deserves a representative and Mr. Rowe will undoubtedly be nominated and elected.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton declines to run for commissioner from precinct No. 1 and backs D. C. Rowe.

articles.text: A new scheme for county division is being broached which, if urged at the coming session of the legislative, will probably be carried. For several years the western part of Morton county has been fighting the eastern and the same is true of the eastern and western parts of Stark county. It is now proposed that a new county be formed from the western part of Morton and the eastern part of Stark, with Sims probably as county seat. The rest of the plan is to extend the western boundary of Stark county to a line east of Belfield and include the rest of Villard county in Billings county. There would seem to be no serious cause of objection to this plan, if carried out as proposed, but we scarcely see the animus of the plan, unless it is to curtail the power of Morton county. In any event, the residents of the counties should be consulted about the changing of their boundary lines and the most feasible plan would be to have an expression of their opinions on it at the November election.
articles.summary: A proposed redrawing of Morton, Stark, Villard and Billings county lines.

articles.text: The story comes from Washington that the law officers of the General Land Office are elaborating a plan by which it is hoped that the Northern Pacific will lose its entire land grant from Duluth to Puget's Sound. The Secretary of the Interior lately decided that no land grant road had earned its grant unless a completed plot of the whole road and the land donated had been filed. With this decision for a starting-point it is hoped to declare the whole grant forfeited. This plot is only a continuation of a long persecution to which the Northern Pacific has been subjected and which has been of incalculable harm to the northwest. The government has for several years allowed the Northern Pacific the right of posession and it has, except for a few technicalities, earned the land granted it. The matter should be settled finally and in favor of the road.
articles.summary: General Land Office plan said to aim at forfeiting the Northern Pacific land grant; the paper defends the road.

articles.text: The stockyards strike in Chicago ended Monday by the return of the old men to the ten-hour rule. Tuesday, the 300 or 400 new men employed by Armour concluded that they did not want to stay if the old men came back and a train was sent out to the yards to take them away. The butchers were in the front of the train and Pinkerton's police in the rear. A stop was made outside of the yards and a crowd gathering around, Pinkerton's men fired and it is supposed mortally wounded two men. Telegraphic reports say the crowd was quiet and that the shooting was unprovoked, although the men claim that the crowd fired first. The event is much regretted, as it is the first difficulty of any moment that has been caused by the sfrike. The strikers returned unconditonally, Armour declaring that he would not yield them a point. After their return he voluntarily raised their wages fifty cents a day all around.
articles.summary: End of the Chicago stockyards strike and a shooting by Pinkerton men.

articles.headline: The Plague, And How to Escape From it.
articles.text:
The animal industries of the United States are in imminent peril from the ravages of an insidious, contagious and incurable disease in cattle commonly called pleuro-pneumonia or lung plague. Many years ago it obtained lodgment on the Atlantic seaboard from imported cattle, and notwithstanding repeated warnings of the danger to be apprehended from its spread, based upon the experience of European countries that have suffered severely from it, our people blinding themselves to their peril, and by spasmodic and half way measures simply averting the disease for a time in particular localities, have allowed it to spread until it has now obtained a firm foothold in the western States, as well as in a number of the eastern ones; and and it is only a question of a very short time when it will find its way to the immense herds on the western and southwestern ranges, unles radical measures are at once adopted to exterminate it where it already exists, and prevent its communication to other parts of the country. This is a matter that affects not only the raisers and dealers in cattle, farmers, dairymen, and butchers, but every man, woman and child in the country, for it strikes directly at the source of supply of [animal food?]. Allow this disease to spread in [the future?] as it has in the past, and the day is not far distant when the animals affected can be counted by the million and not by the hundred as at present, and it is easy to perceive the effect this will have upon our markets and the scarcity of beef that must be the natural result. For years back efforts have been made in some of the States to stamp out the disease, and some light attempt has been made by Congress to give National directions to these efforts, but unfortunately it has been on the penny-wise and pound foolish principle. Owners of cattle naturally object to having their animals killed without receiving full compensation for them, and the government, both State and National, has failed to make provision to pay for the animals that should be slaughtered to eradicate the contagion. As a consequence temporizing measures have been adopted, animals apparently recovered have been permitted to live and mingle with healthy cattle. A partial quarantine has been established about infected herds that has been so loosely enforced as to be practically of no effect, and numerous experiments of inoculation have been tried. It has been very difficult to educate the people of this country to believe that pleuro-pneumonia was contagious, and harder still to convince them that it was incurable. Many animals that had been but slightly affected, apparently recovered, and to outward appearance to the unprofessional eye, were restored to their normal condition of health, and yet these very animals have been the means of spreading the disease all over the country, and while apparently healthy themselves, were centres of contagion that disseminated the seeds of the plague to hundreds of healthy animals. While acting as an Inspector of the United States Government in 1881, in my report to the Commissioner of Agriculture, I recommended as an ultimatum, without which the disease could never be eradicated, "the killing of all chronic cases no matter how apparently healthy they might be." I arrived at this conclusion from careful observation of the operations of the disease not only in this country, but in England, where I had considerable experience in examining its development and spread. Since that time I have carefully watched the progress of the disease in this country, and have communicated with some of the most eminent scientists and experts in England and the United States, who fully agree that the greatest danger to be apprehended is from these chronic or apparently recovered cases. Prof. G. T. Brown, Royal Veterinary College, London, professional adviser to the British Government on contagious diseases of animals, in answer to an inquiry I addressed to him, says, under date of October 21, 1884: "It is quite impossible to tell at what period recovered animals cease to be capable of communicating pleuro-pneumonia, but we have ample evidence to prove that they are the cause of numerous outbreaks of that disease in various parts of the country; in fact, you may take it to be a matter of absolute certainty that it is quite impossible to stamp out pleuro-pneumonia in any country where the so-called recovered animals are allowed to remain alive." In the face of this testimony, and taken in connection with our own actual experience of the constant spread of the disease and its steady march westward, can we afford to longer close our eyes to the danger that threatens us, and allow all our cattle to be affected, before we awaken to the fact that action, prompt, heroic and effective is needed at once, to avert this dire calamity. See to it then that the laws already in existence are rigidly enforced and new ones enacted to meet the exigencies of the case. Have every animal killed that is or has had the slightest contact with diseased animals. The carcasses of healthy or apparently healthy animals killed by reason of contact can be sent to market after proper inspection to prove that they were not injuriously affected, while those that were infected should be buried or entirely destroyed.

In this way and in no other can the plague be checked, and effectually stamped out. While the present outlay of money to accomplish this may be considerable, yet it will save millions of money in the future, protect the food supply of our country and open the foreign markets which have been closed against us for seven years, by reason of the existence of the disease in this country, and in the end as a matter of investment alone prove of incalculable benefit to the cattle interests of the country, and indirectly be of advantage to all consumers of animal food.

JOHN W. GADSDEN,
M. R. C. V. S. Eng.
articles.summary: Letter by veterinarian John W. Gadsden urging the killing of all cattle exposed to pleuro-pneumonia.

articles.text: Word has been received from T. R. Selmes, attorney for Billings Co.'s taxpayers in the suit resisting taxation by Stark county for county purposes, that the case will be decided by the supreme court not later than February.
articles.summary: T. R. Selmes says the Billings County tax suit against Stark County will be decided by February.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores and wife are still down the river on their hunting trip. Up to yesterday, they had killed six mountain sheep, two elk and several antelope and black and white tailed deer. A bear was seen within twenty or thirty feet, but it was too dark to tackle it.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès and his wife are hunting down the river, with six mountain sheep, two elk and other game killed.

articles.text: In spite of the fact that every one anticipated a shortage of hay, more has been put up in the Bad Lands this year than ever before. The Ref. Car Co., have 240 tons, E. G. Paddock about 200 tons, Munro & Lehmicke about 300 tons and every ranch on the river from fifteen to one hundred tons.
articles.summary: More hay was put up in the Bad Lands this year than ever before.

articles.text: The snow came down in a perfect cloud Tuesday and the ground was covered to a depth of four inches. There is no record of such a storm so early in the season, but it furnishes no basis by which to judge the weather of the coming winter, for if the temperature had only been a few degrees warmer, we would have had a fall rain instead of a snow storm.
articles.summary: Four inches of snow fell Tuesday, the earliest such storm on record.

articles.text: Tommy Smith came in last Saturday from a season's work on the trail and in the British Possessions. He reports that there was plenty of work at good prices. On his return he saw the beginning of a fight between two bands of Indians but as he hadn't lost any Indians he didn't stop to enquire their names. He will winter in Deadwood and return in the spring to the British Possessions.
articles.summary: Tommy Smith returned from trail work in the British Possessions and saw two bands of Indians begin to fight.

articles.text: Last Tuesday, the judges of election for precinct No. 2, met and wrote out the polling list for the precinct. Copies of the list can be found at the Ref. Car Co.'s office, at Ferris' store and at the drug store. These copies are for correction and it will be a kindness if all would take an interest in making the list as nearly perfect as possible.
articles.summary: Precinct No. 2 judges of election prepared the polling list; copies posted for correction.

articles.text: Capt. Alexander Hughes candidate for the Council and E. A. Williams candidate for the House, stopped off in Medora last night on an electioneering tour. They represent the brains of the legislative ticket, while Col. Steele represents the bull-dozing qualities, the whole forming a very strong combination and one that will undoubtedly be elected.
articles.summary: Legislative candidates Hughes and Williams stopped in Medora on an electioneering tour.

Brand: Towers & Gudgell, P.O. Keith, Montana — OX; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
articles.summary: Display ads and cattle-brand directory on page 4, columns 2-7, including Roosevelt's Chimney Butte Ranch (Maltese Cross) brand.

events.date_basis: "25th day of October" stated in notice
events.title: Billings County convention called to nominate county ticket
events.summary: A notice signed "Many Voters" called a convention in the Medora Town hall on October 25 at 2 p.m. to nominate a full county ticket.
events.excerpt: on the 25th day of October, at two p. m., a convention will be held in the Town hall

events.title: Theodore Roosevelt nominated for mayor of New York
events.summary: The paper reported that Roosevelt had been nominated by New York City Republicans for mayor and accepted, and said the job might keep him from the spring round-up.
events.excerpt: Theodore Roosevelt was recently nominated by the Republicans of New York city as their candidate for mayor and has accepted the nomination.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Supt. Green runs for legislature as a Democrat
events.summary: The paper commented that railroad Supt. Green's Democratic candidacy for the legislature puzzled the district's papers and gave him little chance.
events.excerpt: The candidacy of Supt. Green on the democratic ticket for the legislature is a conundrum to every paper in the district.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Billings County divided into three voting precincts
events.summary: The county commissioners divided Billings County into three voting precincts, polling at Tompkins' ranch, the Medora Court House and the Little Missouri Horse Co. home ranch.
events.excerpt: The county has been divided by the commissioners into three voting precincts, by east and west lines.

events.title: Bismarck legislative convention passes over west-Missouri candidate
events.summary: At the Bismarck convention, Alexander Hughes was nominated for council and E. A. Williams and W. F. Steele for the house, and Maj. T. J. Mitchell lost 18 to 17. The paper called it Burleigh County wire-pulling.
events.excerpt: the claims of the west-Missouri country were entirely ignored and Alexander Hughes of Burleigh was nominated for the council

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Howard Eaton declines commissioner race, backs D. C. Rowe
events.summary: Howard Eaton declined to run for commissioner from precinct No. 1 and favored D. C. Rowe of the Beaver creek country.
events.excerpt: He absolutely declines however, and favors D. C. Rowe strongly for the position.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: New county-division scheme proposed
events.summary: A plan was reported to form a new county from western Morton and eastern Stark, with Sims as county seat, and to add the rest of Villard County to Billings.
events.excerpt: A new scheme for county division is being broached

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Land Office move against Northern Pacific land grant reported
events.summary: The paper reported that General Land Office lawyers hoped to have the Northern Pacific's whole land grant declared forfeited, and argued against it.
events.excerpt: it is hoped that the Northern Pacific will lose its entire land grant from Duluth to Puget's Sound.

events.title: Howard Eaton sells three cars of cattle in St. Paul
events.summary: Howard Eaton returned from St. Paul after selling three cars of cattle at $3.25.
events.excerpt: Howard Eaton returned last night from St. Paul, where he sold three cars of cattle for $3.25

events.title: Election day set for November 2
events.summary: The paper noted that election day is November 2.
events.excerpt: Election day, Nov. 2.

events.title: Mrs. Mundy leaves for Helena
events.summary: Mrs. Mundy left for Helena Tuesday night.
events.excerpt: Mrs. Mundy left for Helena Tuesday night.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Sheriff Sebastian of Dickinson very sick
events.summary: Sheriff Sebastian of Dickinson had been very sick for some time.
events.excerpt: Sheriff Sebastian of Dickinson, has been very sick for some time.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Jas. Riley in charge at the tank-house
events.summary: Jas. Riley was at the helm at the railroad tank-house.
events.excerpt: Things at the tank-house look more natural with Jas. Riley at the helm.

events.title: Rider and Nugent expected back from St. Cloud
events.summary: Moses Rider and Robert Nugent were expected back soon from their St. Cloud trip.
events.excerpt: Moses Rider and Robert Nugent are expected soon from their St. Cloud trip.

events.title: W. D. Knight of the Yellowstone Journal passes through
events.summary: W. D. Knight of the Yellowstone Journal passed through Medora.
events.excerpt: W. D. Knight of the Yellowstone Journal passed through Medora yesterday morning.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Rains raise the Little Missouri
events.summary: Recent rains raised the river higher than at any time that summer.
events.excerpt: The recent rains have caused the river to rise until it is higher than it has been this summer.

events.title: Probate Judge Ed. Simmers leaves for Chicago
events.summary: Probate Judge Ed. Simmers left for Chicago, where a business opening awaited him.
events.excerpt: Probate Judge Ed. Simmers left Tuesday morning for Chicago

events.title: Brakeman Ed. James killed at Glendive
events.summary: A brakeman named Ed. James was killed at Glendive by falling between the cars.
events.excerpt: A brakeman named Ed. James was killed at Glendive Tuesday night, by falling between the cars.

events.title: E. G. Paddock returns from Wadena with supplies
events.summary: E. G. Paddock returned from Wadena with a car of vegetables and supplies.
events.excerpt: E. G. Paddock returned from Wadena Saturday night. He brought a car of vegetables and supplies with him.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: W. F. Van Driesche's deer hunting
events.summary: W. F. Van Driesche had been very successful lately in killing deer.
events.excerpt: W. F. Van Driesche is becoming the acknowledged Nimrod of Medora.

events.title: Dr. Cunningham arrives to do dental work
events.summary: Dr. Cunningham arrived and had been busy with dental work since, expecting to leave Friday night.
events.excerpt: Dr. Cunningham arrived Tuesday night and has been busy with dental work since.

events.title: Mrs. Lloyd Roberts reports Lloyd in Cheyenne
events.summary: Mrs. Lloyd Roberts came in from the Sloping Bottom ranch and reported Lloyd was in Cheyenne instead of St. Cloud.
events.excerpt: Mrs. Lloyd Roberts came in yesterday from the Sloping Bottom ranch

events.date_basis: "early this week" in week of Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Fire destroys Howard Eaton's hay and barn near VI ranch
events.summary: Howard Eaton lost fifty tons of hay, a barn and some fencing to fire near the VI ranch.
events.excerpt: Howard Eaton met with a serious loss early this week by the burning of fifty tons of hay, a barn and some fencing near the VI ranch.

events.title: Col. W. F. Steele visits Medora
events.summary: Col. W. F. Steele, Republican legislative nominee from Kidder County, was in Medora looking after his fences.
events.excerpt: Col. W. F. Steele was in Medora Tuesday night.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Harry Tarbell will not return to the Bad Lands
events.summary: Harry Tarbell, a manager of the HT horse brand, decided not to return to the Bad Lands, likely after an uncle's death.
events.excerpt: Harry Tarbell, one of the managers of the HT horse brand, has decided not to return to the Bad Lands.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Billings County tax suit to be decided by February
events.summary: T. R. Selmes, attorney for Billings County taxpayers resisting taxation by Stark County, said the supreme court would decide the case by February.
events.excerpt: the case will be decided by the supreme court not later than February.

events.date_basis: "up to yesterday" (20 Oct); trip ongoing in week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Marquis de Morès and wife on hunting trip
events.summary: The Marquis de Morès and his wife were still hunting down the river and had killed six mountain sheep, two elk and several antelope and deer.
events.excerpt: Marquis de Mores and wife are still down the river on their hunting trip.

events.date_basis: haying season of 1886, reported Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Record hay crop put up in the Bad Lands
events.summary: More hay was put up in the Bad Lands than ever before, including 240 tons by the Ref. Car Co., about 200 by E. G. Paddock and about 300 by Munro & Lehmicke.
events.excerpt: more has been put up in the Bad Lands this year than ever before.

events.title: Early snowstorm covers ground four inches
events.summary: Snow fell Tuesday to a depth of four inches, with no record of such a storm so early in the season.
events.excerpt: The snow came down in a perfect cloud Tuesday and the ground was covered to a depth of four inches.

events.title: Tommy Smith returns from British Possessions
events.summary: Tommy Smith came in from a season's work on the trail and in the British Possessions, having seen the start of a fight between two bands of Indians.
events.excerpt: On his return he saw the beginning of a fight between two bands of Indians

events.title: Precinct No. 2 polling list prepared
events.summary: The judges of election for precinct No. 2 wrote out the polling list; copies were left at the Ref. Car Co.'s office, Ferris' store and the drug store.
events.excerpt: the judges of election for precinct No. 2, met and wrote out the polling list for the precinct.

events.title: Hughes and Williams campaign in Medora
events.summary: Council candidate Capt. Alexander Hughes and House candidate E. A. Williams stopped in Medora on an electioneering tour.
events.excerpt: stopped off in Medora last night on an electioneering tour.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 21 Oct 1886
events.title: Packard closes out Studebaker wagons
events.summary: A. T. Packard offered his stock of Studebaker wagons for cash below the wholesale factory rate.
events.excerpt: To close out the stock of Studebaker wagons now on hand, I will make prices for cash that are lower than the wholesale factory rate.
